personal-training-1: A trainer helps one person move more, safely and on purpose, and the first thing to learn is where the job stops. Scope of practice has three zones, and a client scenario can be placed in each. I compared groups to see what activity might do, and I stated only what the comparison could bear. Read this lesson as the same discipline applied to your own work: say what you can do, what you can do only with someone else, and what you must refer. Place three scenarios in the zones before you read on.

The weekly targets are numbers you can quote: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity, or the vigorous equivalent, or a mix. Learn what counts, and how to combine intensities. When you quote a target to a client, say it is a target for groups, linked to better health, not a promise for one person. I watched what bus workers did and counted their events, and a count is only as good as the way you state it. Convert three mixed weeks into minutes before you move on.

Strength work on two or more days a week, sitting less and starting small are the next three points. Start where the client is and build. The evidence for starting small is that many people stop when they begin too hard. Look at the sedentary behaviour advice and the build rule, and write a first week for a client who does almost nothing. State the limits of the advice: it comes from guidelines for groups, and your client is one person.

Every claim you make to a client rests on some kind of evidence, and the strength of a recommendation is not the same as the certainty of the evidence. Learn what a meta-analysis is, and use the evidence card: what was asked, who was compared, what was measured, what was found, who it speaks for and what it means for this client. Ask who was in the study. A finding about one group may not apply to another, and an observational link is not a cause.
personal-training-2: For most people the benefits of activity far outweigh the risks, and screening exists to find the few who need a doctor first. Learn which risks are common and which are rare, and who is most at risk. I reported that vigorous exercise appeared protective in groups, and I would have you say the same to a client, with its scope. Practise a one-minute opening: the benefit, why you ask, what you will do with the answers.

The 2015 ACSM algorithm uses three pieces of information: whether the person is active, whether they have a known disease, and whether they have signs or symptoms. Learn the definitions, and then the decision rules. Apply the algorithm to three invented clients and write the advice for each. Do not improvise the decision: follow the steps, and when the steps say refer, refer. Frame the referral as a way of starting safely, not a refusal.

The AAPQ, the PAR-Q and the ACSM algorithm are often discussed, and the evidence on them has limits. Compare what each asks and what each decides. Know what to use in practice, and why. A tool is a way of getting the same answer from every client, and the comparison tells you how reliable that answer is. Write one sentence on what you would use and why.

The first meeting builds trust, screens, learns the client's story and takes baseline measures. Use the outline, which is our design, and adapt it. Take simple measures, and know the red flags during any session: stop and refer. Listen first. Take a baseline you can repeat, so that later numbers mean something. Write the stop-and-refer rule on the file.
personal-training-3: The best programme fails if the client stops turning up. Self-determination theory names three needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. Learn the three and give an example of wording that supports autonomy. I wrote my conditions as a hypothesis, not as proven law, and you should hold the evidence in this lesson the same way. Notice what the evidence does not show, and say so.

Motivational interviewing is a counselling method, and the evidence on it has limits, including who delivers it. Learn the core skills the teaching framework gives, and practise reflecting back. Say back what you heard, then check it. I said that the conditions are matters of degree and that the client must perceive them, so the check matters as much as the reflection. Role-play a short conversation and count how many of your turns were reflections.

A goal is a promise about the future, and it must survive real life. Turn an outcome goal into performance and process goals, and add an if-then plan for the day it goes wrong. Use the client's own words. I said what I left out of my claims, and you should say what a goal cannot promise. Write a goal and a plan for the worst week.

Progress tracking is feedback, and feedback supports competence. Decide what to track, how often, and what you will do when things slip. Treat a setback as information. Reflect before you advise. Make sure that the client sees their own progress and that the record is kept in a form they can read.
personal-training-4: A resistance programme has a few levers: load, volume, frequency, effort and exercise choice. Two principles hold them together, specificity and progressive overload. I looked for what different illnesses share, and in training the shared thing is demand: the body responds to what it is asked to do. Name the levers and write which you would change first for a beginner. Note how much change to expect, and say that the figure is for groups.

Which load is best depends on the outcome. Match a load range to strength, power or jumping, and read the evidence for each. Overall intensity is more than the percentage on the bar. A demand that is too large is a stage of exhaustion, and a demand that is too small leads nowhere. Write the load range for a client goal and the evidence you used, and state the limits of that evidence.

Volume is the total work, and the hard set is the most useful unit. Estimate the effect of adding weekly sets, and say what the data can and cannot tell you. A different cut of the data may change the picture, so look at both. Count the weekly sets in a plan you have written. More is not always better: watch for the signs that the client is not recovering.

Proximity to failure is how close a set ends to the point where no more repetitions are possible. Reps in reserve is a way to describe it without a maximal test. Use it with beginners with care, and check the client's understanding. The evidence is limited, so treat the scale as a guide. Record the reps in reserve for each set, and compare with how the client felt.
personal-training-5: A session is a set of choices about which movements, in what order, for how many sets. Choose exercises by movement pattern, and put the most demanding first. Rest enough to do each set well. I raised resistance in sets to a 10-repetition maximum for injured servicemen, and later cut the volume I first advised, so I would have you hold your template as a draft. Write one session and count the sets.

This template is an illustrative starting point for a healthy beginner who has passed screening. Count the weekly sets for each muscle group, and check that they fall within the range. Adapt it to the client in front of you. A plan on paper is a hypothesis, and the first weeks test it. Record what the client did, not what you planned.

Progression means raising the demand a little at a time. Use double progression: add repetitions within a range, then add load. When progress stops, look at sleep, food and stress before you change the programme, and consider a lighter week. If there is pain, stop and refer. Write the rule for raising the load and the rule for holding it.

Strength sessions do not replace aerobic activity. Plan the two together, and use a simple talk test to set the effort. Count the weekly minutes against the targets. Say what you will do when the weekly total is short. Keep the plan simple enough to follow on a bad week.
personal-training-6: Clients ask about protein more than almost anything else. Quote the evidence with its range: a daily target in grams per kilogram, with the uncertainty. Calculate a target for an imagined client, and show the range. Treat nutrition as one more demand on the body, along with training, sleep and work. State the limits of the evidence, and where it comes from groups of people, not the one in front of you.

Protein supplements helped trained people more than novices for fat-free mass, and some details mattered little. Know which subgroup results are strong and which are weak. Write what you would tell a novice and what you would tell a trained client. If the result is weak, say so. A strong claim about a weak result is a mistake you can avoid.

A trainer is not a dietitian. Know which nutrition questions are within scope and which you must refer. Practise the sentence: that is a question for a dietitian or your doctor. Good practice is to give general, evidence-based information and no more. I counted every demand on the body, and a diet plan for a medical condition is a demand you are not trained to size.

The WHO gives specific advice for older adults, for pregnant and postpartum women, and for people with chronic conditions and disability. Adapt the programme, work with the client's clinician, and stay inside your scope. Count the demands in the week: training, work, sleep, illness. Lighten the load when the total is high, and refer when a condition is beyond you. This is not medical advice.
personal-training-cap: The brief is to take a realistic case-study client and produce a complete coaching file for the first eight weeks. The file holds the screening record and decision, the goals, the plan with numbers and the weekly activity. I ranked the sources of confidence, and I would have you build the plan so that the early weeks give the client mastery. Plan for success first: make sure that the client can complete what you set.

The model outline shows the shape of a good file, not the only correct answer. Compare yours with it: screening, goals, eight-week plan, weekly activity, scope note. Check that each week leans on one source of confidence and that the strongest, personal mastery, comes first. Note where your plan differs and why. Put a number in every section.

Review your file against the rubric, then role-play the first consultation with a partner. Mark each criterion with evidence. Check how often a client completed what was planned, since early failure weighs more. Write what to keep and what to fix, and run the consultation again. Encouragement without something the client has done is the weakest source, so tie your feedback to an achievement.
